title: Automated Inventory Schema Evolution
business: Retail logistics firms managing high-frequency inventory updates across distributed regional warehouses.
problem: Manual DDL execution leads to inconsistent database states across environments, causing application deployment failures when code expects columns that do not exist in the production schema.
solution: Database schema migration uses versioned SQL scripts to apply structural changes incrementally. By tracking applied migrations in a dedicated metadata table, the system ensures that every database instance reaches the desired state through an idempotent, repeatable process.
steps: Create a migration tracking table to store the version identifier of the last applied script.
Define structural changes in sequential SQL files prefixed with timestamps or version numbers.
Implement a migration runner that checks the tracking table before executing pending scripts.
Wrap each migration script in a transaction block to ensure atomicity during schema modification.
Verify the final schema state against the application requirements after all scripts execute.
outcome: Consistent database structures across all environments, eliminating deployment drift and reducing manual intervention during release cycles.
limitation: Large-scale schema changes, such as adding a column to a table with millions of rows, can cause table locks that block application traffic; check for lock duration using pg_stat_activity.

code.content:
BEGIN; -- Start transaction for atomicity
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_version (version INT PRIMARY KEY);
ALTER TABLE inventory ADD COLUMN warehouse_id INT; -- Apply structural change
INSERT INTO schema_version (version) VALUES (1); -- Record migration
COMMIT; -- Finalize changes
code.explanation: This demonstrates wrapping a schema change in a transaction and updating a metadata table to track the migration state.
